lesson.title: Last In, First Out: Lists as Stacks
lesson.summary: Using a list's append and pop methods together turns it into a stack, a last-in-first-out structure where the most recently added item is always the first one removed.
lesson.body:
A stack is one of the simplest and most useful data structures in computer science, and Python lists implement one for free once you commit to using only two operations: append to add an item to the end, and pop, called with no argument, to remove and return the item at the end. Because both operations happen at the same end of the list, the last item you added is always the first one you get back out, a behavior abbreviated LIFO, for last in, first out.

```python
stack = []
stack.append('a')
stack.append('b')
stack.append('c')
print(stack)
print(stack.pop())
print(stack)
```

The first print shows ['a', 'b', 'c'], the stack after three pushes. stack.pop() removes and returns 'c', the item added most recently, so it prints 'c'. The final print shows ['a', 'b'], the stack with that last item gone. Notice that pop() with no argument specifically removes from the end, position -1; that is what makes it a stack operation rather than something else, and it is also why it is efficient: removing the last element of a Python list requires no shifting of the other elements, so both append and pop from the end run in O(1) time on average.

Stacks show up constantly once you start looking for them. A classic example is checking whether parentheses in an expression are balanced:

```python
def is_balanced(expr):
    stack = []
    for ch in expr:
        if ch == '(':
            stack.append(ch)
        elif ch == ')':
            if not stack:
                return False
            stack.pop()
    return len(stack) == 0

print(is_balanced('(()())'))
print(is_balanced('(()'))
```

This prints True and then False. Every opening parenthesis is pushed onto the stack; every closing parenthesis pops one off, matching it with the most recent unmatched opening one. If a closing parenthesis shows up with nothing on the stack to match, the expression is unbalanced immediately. If anything is left on the stack once the string ends, some opening parenthesis was never closed. This same push-and-pop pattern underlies undo features in software, the back button in a browser, and how a computer keeps track of function calls in progress, which you will encounter again as recursion in a later unit.
